Janice Goh and I wrote a post for the Posit blog:
[Tiny Doses for Tiny Babies -- How much is too much?](https://posit.co/blog/pharmacometrics-in-r-posit)
It is a hands-on introduction to pharmacometrics for R users who have
never built a pharmacokinetic model. Posit also published a narrated
video walkthrough of the post (above).

## The question

A preterm infant weighing 900 g is having seizures. A doctor has read
that one flat dose of phenobarbital might work for every neonate,
which would save dose calculations at the bedside. Is a flat dose
chosen for the average 1.5 kg baby right for a 900 g baby?

To answer that we use `pheno_sd`, the Grasela and Donn (1985) data set
that ships with nlmixr2. It has 59 infants, 589 doses and only 155
concentrations; most infants have one or two samples.

## What the post covers

- **Why a pharmacokinetic model.** If you have fit a mixed model you
  have done half of this. The mean function is the solution to an ODE,
  and its parameters (clearance and volume) mean something
  physiologically.
- **Writing and fitting the model in nlmixr2.** One R function with
  an `ini({})` block and a `model({})` block, fit with SAEM.
- **Adding body weight.** Allometric weight scaling more than halves
  the between-infant variability, from 38.9% to 19.0% CV on clearance.
- **Simulating both dosing options with rxode2.** Under the flat dose
  the median week-2 concentration falls from 39.4 mg/L at 0.7 kg to
  12.3 mg/L at 3.1 kg, and only 3.3% of the heaviest infants reach the
  15-40 mg/L target. Weight-based dosing keeps about 94-100% of
  simulated infants in the target range across all weights.
- **The wider ecosystem.** babelmixr2, nonmem2rx and monolix2rx for
  working with NONMEM and Monolix, plus PKNCA, PopED, xpose.nlmixr2,
  ggPMX, tidyvpc, shinyMixR and nlmixr2rpt.

A flat dose works for the average infant and fails at the extremes.
This is a teaching example, not dosing guidance. A real neonatal
analysis would also need postnatal age and maturation.

The full code is in the post, so you can run the analysis yourself.
[Read it on the Posit blog](https://posit.co/blog/pharmacometrics-in-r-posit)
or [watch the video](https://youtu.be/ZNHOT_AjmYY).

Thanks to Posit for hosting it, and to Janice for the clinical
framing.
